description: MLMP is a one-person team from San Ramón, Costa Rica — a builder who believes software can help people make better decisions about risks we can’t afford to get wrong. I work across data, engineering and AI, with one rule: every claim must trace back to its source. Everything I build points toward one mission: making life multiplanetary. For Space Apps 2026 I’m here to build something rigorous, honest about its limits, and useful long after the weekend.
summary: PYRION Ω answers a question NASA's Moon Base raises: has anyone ever tested fire in its air? NASA expects the Moon Base and pressurized rovers to hold 30 % oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less, which the challenge says makes materials much more flammable, and its PSI database holds no partial-gravity combustion data. PYRION turns 10,380 test records extracted from 18 of NASA's 24 PSI combustion investigations into one dashboard: enter any cabin atmosphere (ISS, Moon, Mars) and it shows which NASA tests apply, with NASA's own words and DOI, where the tested evidence ends, and which test would close the gap. For the Moon Base it finds no test in lunar gravity in PSI; the closest solid-fuel tests are 7.3 oxygen points lower, in microgravity, and planned FM2 still leaves two corners of the band untested. TARS SI (Traceable Applicability Reasoning System) is the AI that reads your question and explains the answer in labelled layers: what the engine computed, what NASA wrote (each quote checked on its page), and its own reasoning. A fixed-rule engine gives every verdict, so changing the AI never changes the answer. Impact: mission planners and fire-safety researchers see in seconds what evidence exists for a habitat atmosphere and what to test next, and any AI assistant can use PYRION through its MCP server. Evidence for test planning, not a safety assessment.
details:
The problem

NASA expects the Moon Base and pressurized rovers to hold 30 % oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less, which the challenge says makes materials much more flammable. NASA's fire experiments are spread across the PSI database, and NASA states that PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data. PYRION addresses one question: for a given cabin atmosphere, which NASA tests are comparable, and what has not been tested?

Who it is for

• Mission planners and habitat engineers: which PSI tests are comparable to an atmosphere (ISS, Moon, Mars, a rover), each cited by DOI.

• Fire-safety researchers: where the tested evidence ends and which test points are missing. For the Moon Base condition, PSI has no test in lunar gravity, and FM2 as planned leaves two corners of the band untested.

• Students: the 24 PSI combustion investigations in one place, each value linked to its NASA source.

• AI assistants: an MCP server at https://pyrion.us/api/mcp exposes the same engine to Claude, ChatGPT and other clients. It offers 19 read-only tools, 5 prompts and 3 resources.

What it does

• Envelope: a verdict for each PSI investigation (applicable, extrapolation, insufficient evidence, or not comparable), with the NASA quote and DOI.

• Worked Example: the Moon Base and ISS cabin air, step by step.

• Mission Planner: coverage of a Moon Base band (a PYRION convention built from NASA atmospheres), what FM2 as planned would measure, and a cited gap report.

• Evidence gaps: the value PSI would need to state for a test to become comparable.

• Investigations: variables, publications and DOIs for the 24 PSI combustion investigations.

TARS SI (Traceable Applicability Reasoning System)

The AI assistant. Each answer is split into labelled layers:

• ENGINE: what the engine computed, by code.

• NASA SAID IT: quotes, each checked by code against the page it cites.

• TARS's own reasoning: labelled as not verified.

Numbers the model writes without a source are removed before display. A model from a different family can review the answer. Verdicts come from the fixed-rule engine, not from the model, so changing the model does not change the verdict or its SHA-256 fingerprint. TARS runs on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, with NVIDIA's free endpoint as fallback. Without any model, the verdicts, dashboard and MCP server still work.

How it works

1. Data: 10,380 condition records extracted from NASA PSI files. 9,650 of the values used as evidence are located by code in the source, as a table cell or a word-for-word quote. 668 are flagged as insufficient.

2. Engine (TypeScript): gravity, fuel phase, diluent and flame type act as barriers. Oxygen and pressure are compared with the region the tests covered.

3. Testing: a battery of 42 questions written by the team, 11 of them traps, runs against the live app. Results are on the Proof page.

Limits

• "Covered" means the condition lies between measured tests, not that a test was run at that point.

• PYRION does not predict lunar fire behaviour and does not call any condition safe.

• The band and tolerances are PYRION conventions, labelled as such.

• Reviews were done by AI reviewer agents, not by NASA or domain experts.

Built with

TypeScript, Next.js and Python. Open source under Apache-2.0: https://github.com/Lucyyngceo/pyrion
